physicalLocation: Upstream basin behind the dam crest, extending to the watershed valley limits.
purpose: Store river inflow and maintain an elevated water surface (headwater elevation) creating gravitational potential energy and regulating seasonal/diurnal flow variability.
engineeringPrinciple: Gravitational potential energy per unit volume $E_{\text{pot}}/V = \rho g \Delta z$ and hydrostatic pressure head relative to tailwater elevation ($H_{\text{gross}} = Z_{\text{headwater}} - Z_{\text{tailwater}}$).
constructionAndMaterials: Natural valley topography bounded by engineered shoreline stabilization, upstream riprap protection, bathymetric silt basin, and reinforced concrete dam face.
operatingMechanism: Inflow from upstream tributaries fills the storage volume between Minimum Operating Level (MOL) and Full Supply Level (FSL); withdrawal through the intake lowers stored volume according to hydrological balance ($\Delta V/\Delta t = Q_{\text{in}} - Q_{\text{turbine}} - Q_{\text{spill}} - Q_{\text{evap}}$).
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Drawdown affects available gross head ($H_{\text{gross}}$) and downstream turbine efficiency; thermal stratification and dissolved oxygen gradients near deep intakes.
potentialFailureModes: Reservoir sedimentation reducing live storage
shoreline slope instability/landslides causing impulse waves
eutrophication or floating debris accumulation
maintenanceConsiderations: Periodic bathymetric silt surveys, debris skimming, water quality monitoring, and watershed inflow gauging
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* Water does not generate electricity simply by moving fast horizontally—elevation difference above the turbine creates usable hydraulic head. *Simplified representation:* DENRYU visualizes a cutaway upstream reservoir slice and parameterizes effective head directly as `Net Head (H)` in the simulator rather than simulating multi-year reservoir hydrology.

engineeringParameters.label: DENRYU illustrative reference `~485 m` ASL yielding `90 m` gross
engineeringParameters.valueText: DENRYU illustrative reference `~485 m` ASL yielding `90 m` gross head above tailwater)

physicalLocation: Across the river gorge between the reservoir and downstream valley.
purpose: Safely impound reservoir water, resist hydrostatic, uplift, and seismic forces, and provide structural integration for the intake and spillway.
engineeringPrinciple: Static equilibrium against overturning and sliding ($F_{\text{hydrostatic}} = \frac{1}{2} \rho g h^2 L$); concrete gravity section transfers horizontal water thrust downward into bedrock foundation via self-weight and friction/shear keys.
constructionAndMaterials: Mass concrete or roller-compacted concrete (RCC) in stepped monolith blocks with vertical waterstops, internal inspection/drainage galleries, foundation grout curtain, and relief drains.
operatingMechanism: Passive civil structure continuously balancing fluctuating hydrostatic thrust, pore uplift pressure along the foundation interface, and thermal expansion/contraction across monolith joints.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Monitoring foundation uplift pressure, seepage flow rates in drainage galleries, and piezometric levels during high-pool events.
potentialFailureModes: Excessive foundation uplift reducing shear resistance
alkali-silica reaction (ASR) concrete swelling
monolith joint waterstop leakage
overtopping during extreme probable maximum flood (PMF)
maintenanceConsiderations: Continuous instrumentation telemetry (pendulums, piezometers, weirs), concrete crack grouting, gallery drain cleaning, and periodic dam safety inspections
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* The dam creates the vertical elevation drop required for high head while absorbing millions of kilonewtons of horizontal water thrust. *Plant-specific note:* DENRYU depicts a concrete gravity dam; other real sites use arch dams, buttress dams, or earth/rockfill embankments depending on valley geology.

engineeringParameters.label: factor of safety against sliding/overturning
engineeringParameters.valueText: factor of safety against sliding/overturning (governed by USBR/USACE dam safety standards).

physicalLocation: Submerged on the upstream face of the dam or adjacent abutment below Minimum Operating Level.
purpose: Draw water smoothly from the reservoir into the conveyance conduit with minimal hydraulic entrance loss, zero air-entraining vortices, and controlled shutoff capability.
engineeringPrinciple: Streamlined bellmouth contraction minimizes flow separation and entrance loss ($h_e = K_e \frac{v^2}{2g}$, typically $K_e \approx 0.04–0.10$); adequate submergence depth ($S > S_{\text{critical}}$) prevents surface air-core vortex formation.
constructionAndMaterials: Reinforced concrete bellmouth piers, curved transition throat, embedded steel gate slots, stoplog guides, and air-vent shaft downstream of the gate slot.
operatingMechanism: Hydrostatic pressure drives water past the trash rack and bellmouth into the headrace/pressure tunnel whenever the intake gate is open and downstream turbine demand exists.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Avoid low-submergence operation that draws air pockets into the penstock (causing slug flow and pressure surges).
potentialFailureModes: Air-entraining vortex ingestion
concrete cavitation or erosion at sharp gate slot edges
submerged silt blockage during low reservoir levels
maintenanceConsiderations: Underwater ROV/diver inspection of concrete bellmouth surfaces, air vent clearing, and stoplog seal inspection
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* Accelerating stationary reservoir water smoothly into a pressurized pipe requires a curved bellmouth—sharp square entrances cause turbulence and permanent energy loss before water even enters the tunnel.

engineeringParameters.label: Design intake velocity
engineeringParameters.valueText: Design intake velocity (`~1.5–3.0 m/s` typical at trash rack/throat, plant-dependent)

physicalLocation: Outer upstream entrance plane of `comp-water-intake`.
purpose: Intercept logs, ice, rocks, aquatic vegetation, and solid debris before water enters the hydraulic conveyance and Francis runner passages.
engineeringPrinciple: Mechanical bar-screen filtration sized with low approach velocity ($v_{\text{approach}} \le 1.0–1.5\ \text{m/s}$) and streamlined bar profiles to limit differential head loss ($\Delta h_{\text{rack}} = K_{\text{bar}} (t/b)^{4/3} (v^2/2g) \sin\alpha$, Kirschmer's formula).
constructionAndMaterials: Galvanized or stainless structural steel flat/teardrop bars welded to horizontal support frames seated in concrete intake guides, often paired with mechanical trash-rack rakes.
operatingMechanism: Stationary barrier; differential head sensors upstream and downstream monitor clogging buildup and trigger raking cycles.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Heavy storm inflows can rapidly load racks with leaves/wood; excessive differential pressure can buckle bars if uncleaned.
potentialFailureModes: Structural collapse under severe debris blockage
flow-induced bar vibration (vortex shedding) causing weld fatigue
corrosion pitting
maintenanceConsiderations: Automated or crane-mounted trash raking, differential pressure instrument calibration, periodic underwater coating/weld inspection
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* A single submerged log passing through high-velocity penstock water can jam guide vanes or fracture curved Francis runner blades; trash racks safeguard the entire plant while keeping velocity low enough to minimize head loss.

engineeringParameters.label: Clear bar spacing
engineeringParameters.valueText: Clear bar spacing (plant-dependent, typically `50–150 mm` for medium-head Francis units)

physicalLocation: Vertical gate shaft immediately downstream of the intake bellmouth inside the dam or intake tower.
purpose: Isolate the headrace tunnel and penstock from the reservoir for dewatering, maintenance, and emergency overspeed/pipe-rupture closure.
engineeringPrinciple: Vertical rectangular steel leaf guided on low-friction rollers or slide bearings, actuated by hydraulic hoists or wire-rope winches; seals under full hydrostatic reservoir pressure against embedded steel frames.
constructionAndMaterials: Welded structural carbon steel skin plate and horizontal box girders, stainless-steel sealing seats, elastomeric J-seals, hydraulic cylinder hoist at deck level, and bypass filling valve.
operatingMechanism: Normally held fully raised out of the flow path during generation. Before opening against an empty penstock, a small bypass valve floods the conduit to equalize hydrostatic pressure across the gate leaf; in emergency closure, gravity + hydraulic thrust drives closure against flowing water.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Never crack-open an un-equalized gate under high head (risk of seal tearing and cavitation); ensure downstream air-vent pipe remains open during draining to avoid vacuum collapse of the conduit.
potentialFailureModes: Damaged elastomer seals causing leakage
gate jamming in debris-fouled slots
hydraulic hoist cylinder leakage
failure to seat during emergency shutdown
maintenanceConsiderations: Periodic stroke testing, seal replacement during planned outages, hydraulic fluid sampling, and slot guide lubrication
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* Unlike `comp-guide-vanes` (which throttle flow continuously during generation), the intake gate is an upstream isolation safety barrier—always wide open in normal operation and closed only for emergency shutoff or conduit inspection.

engineeringParameters.label: closure time
engineeringParameters.valueText: closure time (plant-dependent, emergency shutoff typically `30–120 s`)

physicalLocation: Integrated across the central or flank crest bays of `comp-dam`, discharging down a concrete chute into the river below.
purpose: Safely pass excess floodwaters around the powerhouse when reservoir inflow exceeds storage capacity and turbine discharge, preventing dam overtopping.
engineeringPrinciple: Controlled weir hydraulics ($Q_{\text{spill}} = C_d L H_s^{3/2}$ for free crest flow, or submerged orifice flow under radial tainter gates) paired with an ogee profile matching the lower nappe of a free-falling jet to avoid negative pressure cavitation, ending in a hydraulic-jump stilling basin to dissipate kinetic energy safely.
constructionAndMaterials: High-strength abrasion-resistant concrete ogee crest and chute, training walls, radial steel tainter gates (or gated crest piers), and concrete baffle blocks / flip bucket / stilling basin at the toe.
operatingMechanism: Radial gates lift incrementally in balanced bay sequences during flood events to release excess water while maintaining safe reservoir water level.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Symmetric gate opening prevents asymmetric cross-currents and riverbed scour in the downstream channel; spilled water represents bypassed potential energy that produces zero electricity.
potentialFailureModes: Chute concrete cavitation/erosion at surface irregularities
radial gate trunnion friction corrosion
downstream toe scour undermining the stilling basin
maintenanceConsiderations: Post-flood chute and stilling basin inspections, gate trunnion lubrication, hoist wire/cylinder inspection, concrete surface repair
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* A spillway protects structural survival of the dam during floods by safely converting massive gravitational potential energy into harmless turbulence inside a stilling basin instead of letting water overtop the dam crest.

physicalLocation: Immediately downstream of `comp-intake-gate`, leading water away from the dam intake toward the pressure tunnel / hillside conveyance.
purpose: Convey low-pressure water from the intake structure toward the high-gradient pressure tunnel with minimum friction loss.
engineeringPrinciple: Incompressible closed-conduit or covered-channel steady flow governed by continuity ($Q = A v$) and Darcy-Weisbach head loss ($h_f = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{v^2}{2g}$).
constructionAndMaterials: Reinforced concrete box or circular conduit with smooth troweled interior finish to minimize Manning/Darcy friction roughness.
operatingMechanism: Operates full under moderate reservoir static pressure head; transitions smoothly into the rock-bored or buried pressure tunnel.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Keep velocity moderate so friction losses remain small relative to total head; ensure slow filling during commissioning to purge air pockets.
potentialFailureModes: Concrete joint leakage, longitudinal cracking under internal pressure surges, internal biofilm/silt roughness buildup increasing friction loss
maintenanceConsiderations: Dewatered internal visual walkdown during major multi-year outages, joint sealant renewal
educationalExplanation: *Plant-specific note:* In compact dam-toe powerhouses, the intake connects almost directly to a short embedded penstock; in longer terrain layouts (modeled here for full educational clarity), a headrace and pressure tunnel carry water horizontally before the steep penstock drop.

engineeringParameters.label: illustrative `~4.8 m` equivalent diameter yielding `~3.3 m/s` at
engineeringParameters.valueText: illustrative `~4.8 m` equivalent diameter yielding `~3.3 m/s` at `60 m³/s`)

physicalLocation: Underground/hillside conduit connecting the headrace to the surge tank base and top of the steep penstock.
purpose: Transport pressurized water horizontally through terrain toward the powerhouse drop while withstanding internal hydrostatic pressure and transient surges.
engineeringPrinciple: Pressurized conduit flow governed by Bernoulli's equation with Darcy-Weisbach friction loss ($H_{\text{total}} = z + \frac{p}{\rho g} + \frac{v^2}{2g}$); surrounding rock mass and concrete/steel liner share internal hoop tension.
constructionAndMaterials: Excavated rock tunnel lined with reinforced concrete (or steel lining near low-cover zones and bifurcations) with contact/consolidation grouting into rock.
operatingMechanism: Continuously pressurized column of water transferring fluid mass toward the penstock; elastic water inertia in this long conduit is precisely why a surge tank is required downstream.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Rapid turbine gate closure decelerates the entire tunnel water column ($\Delta p = \rho a \Delta v$ Joukowsky limit if unprotected), producing high transient pressures unless relieved at the surge tank.
potentialFailureModes: Unlined rockfall/spalling
concrete liner longitudinal cracking causing external groundwater exfiltration
unvented air accumulation at high points
maintenanceConsiderations: Periodic dewatered tunnel inspection, rock-trap cleanout upstream of penstock transition, seepage monitoring
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* Water traveling at `~3–4 m/s` inside a long pressure tunnel carries immense momentum—thousands of metric tons of moving mass that cannot stop instantaneously without severe pressure spikes.

physicalLocation: Vertical cylindrical shaft rising near the junction between `comp-pressure-tunnel` and `comp-penstock`.
purpose: Protect the pressure tunnel and penstock from destructive water-hammer pressure surges during rapid turbine load rejection or startup, and supply rapid transient water volume during load acceptance.
engineeringPrinciple: Mass oscillation and pressure-wave reflection. When `comp-guide-vanes` close quickly, moving water in the pressure tunnel diverts upward into the open-surface surge tank, converting kinetic energy into temporary potential elevation ($\Delta z_{\text{surge}}$) and reflecting negative pressure waves back rather than hammering the upstream tunnel; governed by Thoma stability criterion ($A_{\text{st}} > A_{\text{Thoma}}$) for damped oscillations.
constructionAndMaterials: Vertical reinforced concrete or steel-lined shaft extending above maximum reservoir level (with spillway overflow or upper/lower expansion chambers in throttled/differential designs).
operatingMechanism: During steady generation, tank water level sits at reservoir elevation minus tunnel friction head loss. On sudden turbine gate closure, level rises above reservoir elevation and oscillates before damping out; on sudden gate opening, tank supplies immediate water acceleration while tunnel flow catches up.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Maintain free air venting at top of tank; ensure orifice port remains unobstructed; verify governor opening/closing times align with Thoma stability margin.
potentialFailureModes: Downsurge dropping below tunnel crown and drawing air into the penstock
overflow spills
concrete liner spalling from cyclic hydraulic pressures
orifice erosion
maintenanceConsiderations: Water-level transducer calibration, inspection of top vent screens, concrete surface inspection during shutdowns
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* Think of a surge tank as a hydraulic shock absorber and local buffer—it converts high-speed water-hammer pressure spikes into slow, harmless vertical sloshing inside an atmospheric shaft.

engineeringParameters.label: maximum upsurge/downsurge elevations
engineeringParameters.valueText: maximum upsurge/downsurge elevations (must stay below top spill and above tunnel crown to prevent air ingestion).

physicalLocation: Inclined or vertical steel pressure conduit descending from the surge tank / tunnel transition down to the powerhouse main inlet valve.
purpose: Channel pressurized water steeply downward into the Francis turbine while safely containing full static + dynamic hydrostatic pressure and accelerating flow toward the spiral casing.
engineeringPrinciple: Hydrostatic & hydrodynamic pressure containment ($\sigma_{\text{hoop}} = \frac{p D}{2 t}$); internal pressure increases sharply with vertical descent ($p \approx \rho g h_{\text{static}} - \rho g h_f$ during flow). Net head entering the turbine equals gross head minus friction and minor bend losses ($H_{\text{net}} = H_{\text{gross}} - \Delta H_{\text{loss}}$).
constructionAndMaterials: High-tensile welded structural steel plates (e.g., ASTM A516/A537 or EN S355 equivalents, plant-dependent), circumferential external stiffener rings, concrete anchor blocks at bends, saddle supports, expansion joints, and internal epoxy anti-corrosion lining.
operatingMechanism: Continuously conveys pressurized flow from upper conveyance into the turbine inlet; converts elevation drop directly into high static pressure head at the powerhouse floor.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Monitor expansion joints, concrete saddle movement, and drain valves; prevent vacuum conditions during rapid shutdowns via upstream air-admission valves.
potentialFailureModes: External corrosion or internal lining delamination
fatigue cracking at bifurcation or circumferential welds
water-hammer overpressure rupture if guide vanes slam faster than design
buckling under accidental internal vacuum
maintenanceConsiderations: Ultrasonic thickness gauging, weld non-destructive testing (NDT), internal epoxy recoating, expansion gland repacking, anchor block drain checks
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* As water descends the penstock, gravitational elevation drops while internal fluid pressure rises enormously—delivering concentrated hydraulic power ($P_h = \rho g Q H$) right to the turbine entrance. *Assumed simplification:* In DENRYU's simulator, the user directly controls `Net Head (H)` (head already accounting for penstock friction loss), while the Physics & Insights views explain the gross-to-net head loss relationship.

engineeringParameters.label: Internal diameter
engineeringParameters.valueText: Internal diameter (illustrative `~3.4 m`, accelerating velocity to `~6.6 m/s` at `60 m³/s`)

engineeringParameters.label: design internal pressure
engineeringParameters.valueText: design internal pressure (`~1.0–1.4 MPa` class at `~85–100 m` head)

physicalLocation: Inside the powerhouse turbine valve pit immediately upstream of `comp-spiral-casing`.
purpose: Provide positive, watertight isolation of the turbine unit from the pressurized penstock during unit shutdown, maintenance, and emergency runaway protection without draining the entire penstock.
engineeringPrinciple: Quarter-turn mechanical valve disc (lattice/through-flow butterfly valve for medium heads ~`50–150 m`, or full-bore rotary spherical valve for higher heads) rotated `90°` by a hydraulic servomotor and/or counterweight closure system; sealed by pressurized service-water or elastomer maintenance/service seals.
constructionAndMaterials: Cast or welded steel valve body, streamlined lens-shaped butterfly disc (or spherical rotor plug), stainless-steel trunnion shafts and self-lubricating bronze bushings, hydraulic actuation cylinder, counterweight arm, and upstream/downstream bypass equalization pipe.
operatingMechanism: Held fully open (`0°` alignment parallel to flow) during normal generation to minimize head loss. During startup, bypass valve equalizes spiral casing pressure to penstock pressure before main actuator opens the disc. During emergency shutdown or guide vane failure, counterweight/hydraulic pressure closes the valve safely against flow.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Never operate main actuator with high differential pressure unless engineered for emergency flow cut-off; monitor seal leakage during standstill to avoid turbine creeping.
potentialFailureModes: Trunnion bearing seizure
inflatable/mechanical seal failure causing spiral casing leakage at standstill
bypass valve blockage preventing startup equalization
hydraulic actuator seal leak
maintenanceConsiderations: Periodic partial-stroke exercising, seal replacement during unit overhaul, hydraulic oil cleanliness checks, bypass strainer cleaning
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* Draining a long steel penstock takes hours and wastes water; the main inlet valve right outside the turbine allows engineers to isolate the Francis unit in under a minute while keeping the penstock full and pressurized. *Plant-specific note:* Medium-head units (~85 m) typically use streamlined butterfly valves, whereas very high-head units (> 200 m) use zero-obstruction spherical valves.

engineeringParameters.label: Nominal bore diameter
engineeringParameters.valueText: Nominal bore diameter (matching spiral casing inlet, illustrative `~3.0–3.2 m`)

engineeringParameters.label: full-flow head loss coefficient
engineeringParameters.valueText: full-flow head loss coefficient ($K_v \approx 0.1–0.25$ for streamlined butterfly)

physicalLocation: Surrounding the outer perimeter of the stay ring and Francis runner pit inside the powerhouse substructure.
purpose: Distribute pressurized water uniformly around the full `360°` circumference of the stay vanes and guide vanes with constant radial/tangential inlet velocity and minimal hydraulic loss.
engineeringPrinciple: Conservation of mass and free-vortex angular momentum ($r v_\theta = \text{const}$): as water flows around the spiral and bleeds inward into the turbine periphery, the circular cross-sectional area decreases progressively with azimuthal angle ($A(\theta) \propto (1 - \theta/2\pi)$) so tangential velocity and static pressure remain uniform around the runner perimeter.
constructionAndMaterials: Fabricated welded steel plate segments (forming circular cross-sections wrapped in a snail-shell volute, often partially embedded in powerhouse concrete with compressible cork/foam wrap around upper half to control concrete tensile cracking); welded directly to the cast/welded stay ring.
operatingMechanism: Stationary hydraulic distributor; converts rectilinear pipe flow from the main inlet valve into an axisymmetric inward swirling sheet entering the stay vanes.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Maintain balanced pressure tapping telemetry (Winter-Kennedy index flow taps often installed on spiral casing cross-sections to monitor relative discharge).
potentialFailureModes: Fatigue cracking near the baffle plate / tongue junction
internal erosion-corrosion from silt-laden water
structural concrete-to-steel separation vibration
maintenanceConsiderations: Periodic dewatered internal inspection of welds (especially tongue/nose vane), Winter-Kennedy piezometer port flushing, coating touch-up
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* If pressurized pipe water hit only one side of a turbine wheel, uneven forces would wreck the bearings and waste energy. The tapering snail-shell geometry ensures every single degree around the `360°` intake receives equal flow and swirl.

engineeringParameters.label: design pressure including water-hammer allowance
engineeringParameters.valueText: design pressure including water-hammer allowance (typically `1.3–1.5×` max static head)

engineeringParameters.label: spiral wrap angle
engineeringParameters.valueText: spiral wrap angle (`~345°` to nose baffle).

physicalLocation: Fixed annular ring forming the inner throat of `comp-spiral-casing` immediately outside `comp-guide-vanes`.
purpose: Perform a dual mechanical and hydraulic role: structurally transfer massive axial hydraulic pressure and generator/concrete foundation loads across the water passage, while pre-guiding swirling spiral water smoothly toward the movable guide vanes.
engineeringPrinciple: Hydrofoil column struts aligned along the natural spiral flow angle ($\alpha_0$) to minimize drag and incidence shock while acting as structural tension/compression columns connecting the upper and lower stay-ring crowns against internal spiral pressure.
constructionAndMaterials: Cast or welded structural steel / stainless-clad upper and lower annular crowns joined by `12–24` fixed streamlined hydrofoil vanes (`16–20` typical in medium-head Francis designs).
operatingMechanism: Stationary (non-pivoting); serves as structural backbone holding the head cover, bottom ring, and spiral casing open against pressurized water.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Flow alignment errors at extreme off-design discharges cause trailing-edge vortex shedding (Von Kármán street), occasionally inducing acoustic singing or vane cracking if natural frequencies coincide.
potentialFailureModes: Trailing-edge fatigue cracking from Von Kármán vortex shedding
abrasive sand erosion on leading edges
cavitation pitting in separated wakes
maintenanceConsiderations: Magnetic-particle or dye-penetrant NDT inspection of vane-to-crown fillets during overhauls
trailing-edge profile grinding ("Donaldson chamfer") if singing occurs
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* Stay vanes look similar to guide vanes, which often confuses learners—the critical difference is that stay vanes are **welded fixed structural pillars** carrying immense forces while pre-aligning the swirl, whereas the inner guide vanes **pivot** to control flow.

engineeringParameters.label: Number of stay vanes
engineeringParameters.valueText: Number of stay vanes (typically matches or is half the guide vane count, avoiding harmonic resonance multiples)

engineeringParameters.label: leading-edge inlet angle matching spiral flow angle.
engineeringParameters.valueText: leading-edge inlet angle matching spiral flow angle.

physicalLocation: Concentric annular ring situated immediately between `comp-stay-vanes` and the outer inlet perimeter of `comp-runner`.
purpose: Continuously regulate water flow rate ($Q$) entering the runner, set the optimal tangential swirl velocity ($v_{u1}$) required by the runner blades, and shut off water admission to start, load-control, or stop the unit.
engineeringPrinciple: Pivoting hydrofoil cascade connected via crank arms and shear pins to a hydraulic governor-actuated regulating ring. Changing gate angle $\alpha_1$ simultaneously adjusts throat opening area ($A_{\text{gate}}$) and angular momentum ($r_1 v_{u1}$) entering the runner per the Euler turbomachinery equation ($T = \rho Q (r_1 v_{u1} - r_2 v_{u2})$).
constructionAndMaterials: Precision-machined cast martensitic stainless steel (e.g., CA6NM / 13Cr-4Ni) hydrofoil blades with upper and lower integral trunnion stems rotating in bronze/self-lubricating bushings inside the head cover and bottom ring; linked via levers, breaking links/shear pins, and twin hydraulic servomotors acting on the regulating ring.
operatingMechanism: The turbine governor commands hydraulic servomotors to rotate the regulating ring, pivoting all `20–24` guide vanes synchronously from `0%` (fully closed contact) to `100%` (maximum rated opening). Shear pins fracture intentionally if debris jams a single gate, protecting adjacent linkage.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Operating at very small openings (`< 25–30%`) produces severe throttle turbulence, incidence shock, and draft-tube cavitation vortex rope; gate seals wear over time allowing slight leakage at closed position.
potentialFailureModes: Shear pin breakage from debris jamming
bushing seizure or galling
end-clearance erosion increasing closed-gate leakage
hydraulic servomotor drift
maintenanceConsiderations: Gate-to-gate clearance and facing seal checks, regulating ring linkage greasing, shear pin inspection, governor deadband and stroke-time calibration
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* Guide vanes act as the turbine's throttle AND steering wheel at the same time—they decide both *how much* water enters and *at what angle* it strikes the runner blades.

engineeringParameters.label: opening range
engineeringParameters.valueText: opening range (`0–100%`, nominal BEP around `~75–85%` opening depending on head)

engineeringParameters.label: governor stroke rate limits
engineeringParameters.valueText: governor stroke rate limits (closing time typically `5–12 s` tuned against penstock surge).

physicalLocation: Central rotating core inside the distributor throat (`comp-guide-vanes`), bolted onto the bottom flange of `comp-main-shaft` directly above `comp-draft-tube`.
purpose: Convert the pressure energy and kinetic angular momentum of incoming pressurized water into smooth mechanical shaft torque and continuous rotational power.
engineeringPrinciple: **Reaction + Mixed-Flow Turbomachinery (Euler Turbine Equation):** Unlike an impulse Pelton wheel operating in air, a Francis runner runs completely submerged under pressure. As water flows radially inward and curves axially downward through the narrowing blade passages, both static pressure drops (reaction effect, typically ~50% of energy conversion) and tangential velocity decreases (impulse/angular momentum change), generating shaft torque: $$T = \rho Q (r_1 v_{u1} - r_2 v_{u2}), \qquad P_m = T \omega = \rho g Q H \eta_t$$
constructionAndMaterials: Single-piece cast or fabricated/welded martensitic stainless steel (`13Cr-4Ni` / ASTM A743 CA6NM) consisting of: (1) upper **Crown** (hub bolted to shaft), (2) lower **Band** (shroud ring encircling blade outer tips with labyrinth seal rings), and (3) `13–17` double-curved 3D **Runner Blades** (`comp-runner-blades`) spanning between crown and band.
operatingMechanism: Water enters the outer diameter radially around the full `360°` periphery, transfers angular momentum to the blades while dropping in pressure, and exits axially downward out the runner eye into the draft tube at near-zero residual swirl at Best Efficiency Point (BEP).
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Must stay set below tailwater elevation sufficient to satisfy Thoma cavitation parameter ($\sigma_{\text{plant}} > \sigma_{\text{critical}}$); avoid prolonged operation in rough part-load band (`< 45%` flow) where helical draft-tube vortex rope causes vibration.
potentialFailureModes: Cavitation pitting on low-pressure suction side near trailing edge
high-cycle fatigue cracking at blade-to-crown/band fillets (rotor-stator interaction pressure pulsations)
silt abrasion erosion
labyrinth seal wear increasing volumetric leakage loss
maintenanceConsiderations: Periodic cavitation dye-penetrant NDT, stainless weld-overlay repair and template grinding of pitted blades, labyrinth seal clearance measurements, dynamic balancing checks
educationalExplanation: *Why Francis differs from Pelton & Kaplan:* A **Pelton** runner uses open-air buckets hit by high-velocity water jets (high head, low flow). A **Kaplan** propeller uses flat-pitched axial blades ideal for low heads and huge flows. A **Francis** runner uniquely bridges the middle: water enters **radially** around the edge under full pressure and exits **axially** through the center, giving it signature twisted 3D spoon-shaped blades enclosed between a crown and band.

engineeringParameters.label: specific speed
engineeringParameters.valueText: specific speed ($N_s$, medium-head Francis typically `~120–250` metric $n_{q}$ equivalent `~35–75`)

engineeringParameters.label: synchronous speed
engineeringParameters.valueText: synchronous speed (`250 rpm` in DENRYU 50 Hz 24-pole configuration)

engineeringParameters.label: runaway overspeed capability
engineeringParameters.valueText: runaway overspeed capability (`~1.7–2.1×` synchronous speed per IEC/IEEE mechanical design margins)

physicalLocation: Curved hydrofoil passages welded/cast between the upper crown and lower band of `comp-runner`.
purpose: Extract fluid energy smoothly through continuous aerodynamic/hydrodynamic pressure differential between the pressure (concave) face and suction (convex) face while turning the water `90°` from radial inward to axial downward flow.
engineeringPrinciple: 3D hydrofoil boundary-layer aerodynamics/hydrodynamics and velocity-triangle matching ($w = c - u$): blade inlet angle ($\beta_1$) aligns smoothly with relative water velocity at BEP to avoid shock loss, while trailing-edge twist ($\beta_2$) matches varying peripheral blade speed ($u = \omega r$) from crown to band so exit whirl approaches zero ($v_{u2} \approx 0$).
constructionAndMaterials: `13–17` double-curved hydrofoil blades (illustrative `15` blades—odd/prime-like relative to `20` guide vanes to prevent synchronous pressure-pulse resonance) formed via 5-axis CNC milling or precision investment/sand casting in `13Cr-4Ni` stainless steel.
operatingMechanism: Stationary relative to the runner hub; rotates integrally with `comp-runner`, experiencing steady centrifugal + hydraulic bending loads overlaid by periodic pressure pulses as each blade passes stationary guide vanes.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: At off-BEP flow rates, incoming relative angle mismatches $\beta_1$, causing leading-edge flow separation, eddy losses, and potential suction-side cavitation clouds.
potentialFailureModes: Trailing-edge suction-side cavitation pitting
fillet fatigue cracking from rotor-stator interaction (RSI)
leading-edge sediment erosion
Karman vortex trailing-edge vibration
maintenanceConsiderations: Ultrasonic thickness verification, profile-gauge blade shape checking after weld repairs, polishing suction faces to maintain hydraulic smoothness
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* Notice how a Francis blade twists dramatically from top to bottom—near the outer edge it sits almost vertical to catch radial water cleanly, while near the bottom center it curves nearly horizontal like a fan blade to push water axially downward without wasting rotational energy in the exit swirl.

engineeringParameters.label: Blade count
engineeringParameters.valueText: Blade count (`15` illustrative vs. `20` guide vanes)

engineeringParameters.label: inlet/outlet blade angles
engineeringParameters.valueText: inlet/outlet blade angles ($\beta_1, \beta_2$ varying spanwise from crown to band)

engineeringParameters.label: minimum surface pressure margin against vapor pressure
engineeringParameters.valueText: minimum surface pressure margin against vapor pressure ($p_{\min} > p_v$).

physicalLocation: Vertical central axis extending from the Francis runner hub upward through the turbine head cover seal, intermediate flange coupling, and generator thrust/guide bearings to `comp-rotor`.
purpose: Transmit mechanical torque and rotational power reliably from the submerged turbine runner to the generator rotor while carrying axial hydraulic thrust and shaft weight.
engineeringPrinciple: Torsional shear transmission ($\tau_{\max} = \frac{T r}{J}$, where $P_m = T \omega$) combined with axial compression/tension (total weight of runner + shaft + rotor + hydraulic downward thrust on the crown) and lateral whirling critical-speed stiffness ($n_{\text{critical}} \gg n_{\text{runaway}}$).
constructionAndMaterials: Heavy forged alloy steel (e.g., AISI 4140 / 34CrNiMo6 class) machined with integral forged coupling flanges joined by precision fitted tension bolts, replaceable stainless shaft sleeve through the turbine shaft seal, and polished bearing journals.
operatingMechanism: Rotates synchronously with the runner and generator rotor (`250 rpm` in DENRYU), transferring pure mechanical work upward across the powerhouse floor boundary.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Maintain shaft alignment plumb within strict tolerances; monitor shaft vibration proximity probes (`X-Y` radial orbit); ensure turbine shaft seal prevents powerhouse flooding.
potentialFailureModes: Shaft seal wear/overheating causing water ingress into turbine pit
bearing journal scoring
coupling bolt loosening under torsional shock (short-circuit torque transient)
misalignment-induced cyclic bending fatigue
maintenanceConsiderations: Laser/piano-wire shaft plumbness & coupling runout alignment checks, shaft seal carbon/rubber packing replacement, NDT on flange fillets
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* Even though the shaft simply looks like a thick steel rod, at full load it simultaneously carries hundreds of tons of downward hydraulic thrust and twists under more than a million Newton-meters of torque—yet connects wet fluid mechanics below directly to clean electromagnetism above.

engineeringParameters.label: Shaft torque
engineeringParameters.valueText: Shaft torque ($T = P_m / \omega$, e.g., `~1.74 MN·m` at `45.5 MW, 250 rpm`)

engineeringParameters.label: outer diameter
engineeringParameters.valueText: outer diameter (illustrative `~0.65–0.80 m` solid or hollow-bored)

physicalLocation: Embedded in concrete powerhouse foundation directly underneath `comp-runner`, curving `90°` horizontally out toward `comp-draft-tube-outlet`.
purpose: Recover residual kinetic energy leaving the runner by smoothly decelerating exit water in an expanding diffuser, and enable setting the turbine above tailwater (or recover elevation head down to tailwater) via controlled sub-atmospheric suction pressure.
engineeringPrinciple: **Bernoulli Diffuser Pressure Recovery:** Because cross-sectional area increases steadily from runner exit ($A_2$) to outlet ($A_3$), water velocity drops ($v_3 \ll v_2$), converting dynamic velocity head ($\frac{v_2^2 - v_3^2}{2g}$) back into static pressure recovery so pressure right beneath the runner drops below atmospheric ($p_2 < p_{\text{atm}}$), maximizing effective net head across the runner!
constructionAndMaterials: Upper conical steel liner (stainless-clad near runner throat to resist cavitation pitting) transitioning into a smooth curved `90°` reinforced concrete elbow and horizontally expanding concrete rectangular diffuser channels (often split by concrete splitter piers).
operatingMechanism: Stationary divergent hydraulic passage; runs completely full and submerged below tailwater level at all times during operation to sustain continuous vacuum siphon/pressure recovery without air break.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: At part-load (`40–65%` flow), residual swirl leaving the runner forms an unstable helical **vortex rope** inside the draft tube cone causing `~0.2–0.5 Hz` Rheingans pressure surges and audible thumping; air admission through the runner nose cone is often used industrially to cushion this pulsation.
potentialFailureModes: Throat liner cavitation pitting
vortex-rope fatigue vibration cracking steel-to-concrete anchor ties
uplift/collapse of liner if drained rapidly without exterior drain relief
maintenanceConsiderations: Dewatering via tailrace stoplogs to inspect cone liner, cavitation repair, checking air admission pipe, clearing debris at splitter piers
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* Without a draft tube, water shooting out of the runner would waste up to 10–15% of total head as unused exit kinetic energy AND the plant would lose the elevation head between the runner and the river surface below. The widening elbow gently brakes the water, creating beneficial suction underneath the runner.

engineeringParameters.label: Cone divergence angle
engineeringParameters.valueText: Cone divergence angle (typically `6–10°` total angle to prevent boundary-layer separation)

engineeringParameters.label: submergence elevation relative to tailwater
engineeringParameters.valueText: submergence elevation relative to tailwater (Thoma cavitation setting)

physicalLocation: Inside the vertical generator pit/barrel, mounted concentrically inside `comp-stator` atop `comp-main-shaft`.
purpose: Rotate a multi-pole DC magnetic field smoothly past the stationary armature coils (`comp-stator-winding`) to induce three-phase alternating voltage and provide rotational inertia ($H_{\text{inertia}}$) stabilizing grid frequency.
engineeringPrinciple: Synchronous electromechanical rotation locked to grid frequency: $$n_s = \frac{120 f}{N_p}$$ (e.g., $N_p = 24$ poles at $f = 50\ \text{Hz} \implies n_s = 250\ \text{rpm}$). Low-speed hydraulic turbines require large-diameter, high-pole-count **salient-pole** rotors rather than 2-pole cylindrical steam-turbine rotors.
constructionAndMaterials: Heavy forged steel shaft hub, radial spider arms, laminated high-strength steel rim shrunk/keyed onto spider, and `24` bolted/dovetailed salient pole bodies carrying DC `comp-field-winding` coils plus copper damper (amortisseur) bars embedded in pole shoes, plus upper/lower ventilation fan blades.
operatingMechanism: Driven mechanically by `comp-main-shaft` while energized by DC current from `comp-excitation-system`. Magnetic attraction between the rotating rotor poles and the stator's rotating magnetic field locks rotor speed strictly to grid frequency (`n_s`) during synchronized operation, transmitting load torque across the air gap.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Maintain uniform air gap symmetry (`< 5–10%` eccentricity) to prevent unbalanced magnetic pull (UMP); damper windings suppress hunting oscillations during grid faults.
potentialFailureModes: Rotor rim/pole wedge loosening under centrifugal overspeed cycles
inter-turn field winding shorts causing thermal bowing and vibration
damper bar cracking from negative-sequence currents
maintenanceConsiderations: Air-gap measurement via feeler gauges/capacitive probes, pole-drop impedance testing, wedge tightness taps, brush/slip-ring cleaning, mechanical brake pad inspection on lower rotor brake track
educationalExplanation: *Why hydro rotors look wide and flat:* Unlike 3000-rpm steam turbines, Francis water wheels spin slowly (`~100–600 rpm`). To still produce `50 Hz` or `60 Hz` grid AC, the rotor needs many magnetic north/south pole pairs (`24` poles in DENRYU) arranged around a wide-diameter flywheel rim.

engineeringParameters.label: air gap radial clearance
engineeringParameters.valueText: air gap radial clearance (typically `~12–25 mm` plant-dependent)

physicalLocation: Stationary cylindrical ring encircling `comp-rotor` inside `comp-generator-housing`, bolted down to powerhouse concrete soleplates.
purpose: Provide a low-reluctance laminated magnetic return path for rotating rotor flux, structurally support `comp-stator-winding` against electromagnetic short-circuit torques, and channel cooling air radially through core ducts.
engineeringPrinciple: Alternating magnetic flux passing through steel experiences eddy-current and hysteresis iron losses ($P_{\text{core}} \propto f^{1.3–2} B_{\max}^2$). Constructing the stator core from thin stacked, varnished silicon-steel laminations dramatically limits eddy current circulation and core heating.
constructionAndMaterials: Welded structural steel cylindrical frame with radial support ribs, stacked `0.35–0.5 mm` grain-oriented or low-loss non-oriented electrical silicon-steel core punchings clamped tightly between heavy end-fingers/through-bolts, and axial cooling air spacers creating radial ventilation ducts.
operatingMechanism: Remains strictly stationary while conducting alternating magnetic flux induced by the spinning rotor poles and resisting equal-and-opposite electromagnetic reaction torque directly into the powerhouse foundation.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Core compression clamping pressure must remain tight to prevent lamination fretting ("red-dust" iron oxide powder); avoid over-fluxing ($V/f > 1.05$ p.u.) which saturates core iron and spikes core heating.
potentialFailureModes: Loose core lamination wedges causing vibration and slot insulation abrasion
inter-laminar insulation breakdown creating local hot spots
soleplate thermal expansion distortion causing ovalization
maintenanceConsiderations: ELCID (Electromagnetic Core Imperfection Detection) or rated-flux core ring tests, core-bolt torque checks, RTD core temperature trending, visual bore cleaning
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* The stator is not a solid cast iron pipe—it is assembled from tens of thousands of paper-thin insulated steel sheets stacked together so magnetic fields cross smoothly without turning the frame into a giant induction heater.

engineeringParameters.label: Stator bore diameter
engineeringParameters.valueText: Stator bore diameter (plant-dependent, illustrative `~4.8–5.5 m` for a `45 MW, 250 rpm` vertical hydro unit)

engineeringParameters.label: core iron loss fraction
engineeringParameters.valueText: core iron loss fraction (`~0.3–0.6%` of rated MVA)

physicalLocation: Wound concentrically around each of the `24` salient pole bodies on the outer periphery of `comp-rotor`.
purpose: Produce the steady, controllable DC magnetomotive force (MMF) establishing alternating North-South magnetic poles around the rotor perimeter.
engineeringPrinciple: Ampère's circuital law ($\oint \mathbf{H}\cdot d\mathbf{l} = N I_f$): passing controlled DC excitation current $I_f$ through multi-turn pole coils builds magnetic flux $\Phi_f$ per pole, directly governing induced internal stator EMF ($E_f \propto \omega \Phi_f$) and generator reactive power ($Q_{\text{VAR}}$) output.
constructionAndMaterials: Edge-wound flat copper strap coils (allowing superior heat dissipation on outer edges) or insulated multi-turn rectangular copper conductors, insulated from the steel pole body with Class F/H epoxy-mica/Nomex pole collars and held firmly against centrifugal force by pole shoes and inter-pole V-blocks/braces.
operatingMechanism: Series-connected pole coils alternate winding polarity (`N-S-N-S...` around all `24` poles) fed via rotor leads from `comp-excitation-system`. Increasing $I_f$ boosts magnetic flux, raising terminal voltage (open circuit) or reactive power export (grid-tied).
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Monitor rotor ground-fault protection (single ground usually alarms, second ground shorts turns causing violent magnetic unbalance); respect field thermal overload limits during voltage sags.
potentialFailureModes: Turn-to-turn insulation shorts (causing asymmetric heating and 1× shaft vibration)
copper thermal dusting
lead-wire fatigue at shaft bore transitions
earth fault from carbon/oil contamination
maintenanceConsiderations: Pole-drop AC impedance test, DC winding resistance check, Megger insulation resistance & polarization index (PI), inter-pole brace tightening
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* Unlike tiny bicycle dynamos using permanent magnets, utility hydroelectric generators use **electromagnets** on the rotor. Adjusting the DC current in these field coils lets grid operators regulate station voltage and reactive power cleanly even while turbine speed stays locked to `50 Hz`.

engineeringParameters.label: Rated field current & voltage
engineeringParameters.valueText: Rated field current & voltage (plant-dependent, typically `200–1200 A DC` at `100–400 V DC`)

engineeringParameters.label: insulation thermal class
engineeringParameters.valueText: insulation thermal class (Class F `155 °C` / Class H `180 °C` per IEEE C50.12)

physicalLocation: Embedded inside longitudinal slots around the inner bore of `comp-stator`, with curved end-turns projecting above and below the core iron.
purpose: Serve as the stationary electrical conductor circuit where the rotating rotor magnetic field induces three-phase AC voltage and delivers load current out to the plant electrical system.
engineeringPrinciple: **Faraday's Law of Electromagnetic Induction:** As `24` alternating magnetic poles sweep past spatially `120°`-displaced phase coil groups (`Phase A, B, C`), time-varying magnetic flux linkage ($\lambda(t)$) induces balanced sinusoidal three-phase EMF: $$e(t) = -N \frac{d\Phi}{dt}, \qquad E_{\text{rms}} = 4.44 f N k_w \Phi_f$$ Output electrical power equals active electromagnetic power minus $I^2 R$ stator copper loss and core/stray losses.
constructionAndMaterials: Transposed Roebel copper bars (reduces skin-effect & circulating-current eddy losses inside thick conductors), insulated with high-voltage vacuum-pressure impregnated (VPI) mica-epoxy groundwall tape + semi-conductive corona slot armor, wedged tightly in slots with fiberglass ripple springs and braced at end-turns against short-circuit forces.
operatingMechanism: Stationary conductors carrying high-voltage alternating current (`e.g., 10.5–13.8 kV` line-to-line typical medium-high hydro generator class) out via collector phase rings to `comp-generator-terminal`.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Slot-wedge tightness and end-winding bracing must resist `2×` to `10×` rated current electromagnetic forces during external faults; monitor partial discharge (PD) activity and embedded slot RTD temperatures.
potentialFailureModes: Groundwall mica-epoxy insulation thermal aging or partial-discharge treeing
loose slot wedges causing slot-discharge erosion
end-winding corona or vibration fatigue
cooling blockage overheating conductors
maintenanceConsiderations: Offline Doble power-factor / tan-delta & partial-discharge testing, hi-pot withstand tests, end-winding bump tests, RTD checks, borescope inspection of wedging
educationalExplanation: *Why stator carries the high power instead of the rotor:* Putting `11 kV` and thousands of amperes on the **stationary** stator avoids pushing gigantic power currents through sliding carbon brushes—only modest DC excitation current goes to the spinning rotor!

engineeringParameters.label: Rated line-to-line terminal voltage
engineeringParameters.valueText: Rated line-to-line terminal voltage (`10.5–13.8 kV` typical class, plant-dependent

engineeringParameters.label: rated current
engineeringParameters.valueText: rated current (`~2.4–2.6 kA` per phase at `~45–50 MVA`)

engineeringParameters.label: stator copper loss
engineeringParameters.valueText: stator copper loss ($\propto I^2 R$, dominant load-dependent loss term in generator efficiency curve).

physicalLocation: Auxiliary floor cubicle beside/above the generator housing plus collector slip-ring brush gear (or brushless exciter assembly) on top of the shaft.
purpose: Supply regulated DC current to `comp-field-winding` and automatically control terminal voltage, reactive power factor, and transient power-system stability via the Automatic Voltage Regulator (AVR) and Power System Stabilizer (PSS).
engineeringPrinciple: Closed-loop feedback voltage/reactive power control: measures stator terminal voltage ($V_t$) via potential transformers (PTs), compares against setpoint, and modulates SCR thyristor firing angles (static excitation drawing from an excitation transformer) to raise or lower DC field current $I_f$ within milliseconds.
constructionAndMaterials: Thyristor rectifier bridge cabinets, digital AVR/PSS controller racks, DC field circuit breaker & crowbar discharge resistor, excitation power transformer, and shaft-mounted copper/steel collector slip rings with carbon brush rigging (for static systems).
operatingMechanism: During startup, field flashing builds initial voltage from station DC batteries until self-excitation takes over; during grid operation, AVR continuously compensates armature reaction as electrical load varies while respecting under-excitation (stator end-iron heating) and over-excitation (field thermal) limiters.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: De-excitation crowbar must safely dissipate stored inductive rotor magnetic energy ($\frac{1}{2} L_f I_f^2$) within seconds during an internal generator electrical fault trip.
potentialFailureModes: Carbon brush arcing/rapid wear on collector rings
thyristor bridge fuse failure or cooling fan fault
AVR feedback PT loss causing dangerous over-excitation trip
field breaker contact welding
maintenanceConsiderations: Brush length/spring-tension replacement, slip-ring surface turning/cleaning, AVR calibration & step-response testing during planned outages, rectifier cabinet filter cleaning
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* Many students think spinning the turbine faster increases voltage—no! On a grid-tied generator, speed MUST stay fixed at synchronous speed (`250 rpm`). Instead, the **excitation system** acts like a magnetic dimmer switch, adjusting rotor magnetism to control voltage and reactive power.

engineeringParameters.label: Ceiling voltage ratio
engineeringParameters.valueText: Ceiling voltage ratio (typically `1.6–2.0×` rated field voltage for transient grid stability)

engineeringParameters.label: response time
engineeringParameters.valueText: response time (`< 50 ms` for static thyristor systems)

physicalLocation: Upper/lower generator bearing brackets surrounding `comp-main-shaft` (combining an axial **Thrust Bearing** above or below the rotor and radial **Guide Bearings** along the shaft).
purpose: Support the entire vertical axial weight of the rotating assembly plus downward hydraulic water thrust on the runner while maintaining concentric radial alignment of the rotor inside the narrow stator air gap with ultra-low friction.
engineeringPrinciple: **Hydrodynamic Tilting-Pad Oil-Film Lubrication (Reynolds Equation):** As the rotating thrust collar drags oil into tapered wedge clearances under self-pivoting white-metal (Babbitt) pads, fluid film pressure rises enough to float hundreds of metric tons of rotating mass on an oil film roughly `30–80 µm` thick with zero metal-to-metal contact once running. High-pressure oil-jacking lift pumps inject oil beneath pads during low-speed startup/shutdown before the hydrodynamic wedge forms.
constructionAndMaterials: Cast/fabricated steel bearing housing oil pot, mirror-finished forged steel thrust runner collar, pivoted Babbitt-lined (tin-antimony-copper alloy) or PTFE-faced tilting pads mounted on spherical pivots/springs, immersed water-cooled copper/stainless oil-cooler coils, high-pressure startup oil-lift pump manifold, and embedded pad RTDs.
operatingMechanism: Stationary oil bath and self-pumping collar grooves circulate turbine oil continuously past tilting shoes and water-cooled heat exchangers; guide bearing pads center radial shaft runout within microns.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Never run below minimum speed without high-pressure lift oil active (risk of wiping soft Babbitt surface); verify electrical shaft-current insulation on upper bearing bracket to prevent EDM bearing pitting.
potentialFailureModes: Babbitt pad wiping due to oil-lift failure or cooling loss
water contamination emulsifying bearing oil
shaft-voltage circulating currents causing electrical pitting
oil seal vapor leakage contaminating stator windings
maintenanceConsiderations: Periodic oil viscosity/moisture/wear-metal lab analysis, pad clearance & contact-pattern checking, oil-cooler pressure testing, shaft-grounding brush maintenance
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* How do you hang 300+ tons spinning at 250 rpm without grinding metal into dust? Tilting-pad bearings use clever wedge geometry so the spinning shaft itself pumps pressurized oil underneath its shoes, levitating the entire rotor-turbine stack on a film of oil thinner than a sheet of paper.

engineeringParameters.label: Axial thrust load capacity
engineeringParameters.valueText: Axial thrust load capacity (hundreds of metric tons, plant-dependent)

engineeringParameters.label: normal Babbitt pad operating temperature
engineeringParameters.valueText: normal Babbitt pad operating temperature (`~55–75 °C`, alarm `~85–90 °C`, trip `~95–100 °C`)

engineeringParameters.label: mechanical friction loss
engineeringParameters.valueText: mechanical friction loss (`~0.2–0.5%` of unit output, factored into `generatorEfficiency` / mechanical windage-friction).

physicalLocation: Finned radiator coolers mounted symmetrically around the outer circumference of `comp-stator` inside `comp-generator-housing`, plus cooling water manifolds to `comp-bearings`.
purpose: Continuously remove heat generated by stator copper $I^2R$ losses, stator iron core losses, rotor field $I^2R$ losses, windage drag, and bearing friction so electrical insulation and bearing Babbitt remain well within safe thermal limits.
engineeringPrinciple: Forced closed-loop air convection + water-cooled heat exchange ($Q_{\text{heat}} = \dot{m}_{\text{air}} c_p \Delta T_{\text{air}} = U A \Delta T_{\text{lm}}$): rotor spider arms and fan blades pump warm air outward through rotor poles, across the air gap, through radial stator core ducts, and out through circumferential finned air-to-water heat exchangers before recirculating cool air back to rotor top/bottom.
constructionAndMaterials: Radial cupronickel or stainless-steel finned-tube air-to-water heat exchanger banks bolted onto outer stator frame openings, closed-loop cooling water booster pumps, strainers, thermostatic control valves, and river/penstock raw-water secondary heat exchangers.
operatingMechanism: As electrical load increases, stator $I^2R$ losses rise quadratically ($I^2 R$), raising generator air temperature; modulated cooling water flow through finned coils maintains cold air inlet around `~35–40 °C` and avoids moisture condensation during cold standby.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Maintain cooling water pressure slightly lower or carefully monitored against leakage inside generator pit; prevent biological fouling or silt buildup inside finned tubes.
potentialFailureModes: Tube fouling/scaling reducing heat transfer and triggering stator over-temperature derating
cooling water tube leak spraying moisture onto high-voltage windings
raw-water strainer blockage
maintenanceConsiderations: Automated backwash strainer flushing, seasonal acid/mechanical tube descaling, hydrostatic leak testing of exchanger headers, flow-switch alarm verification
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* Even at an impressive `97%` generator efficiency, a `45 MW` hydro generator converts roughly `1.4 MW` of mechanical input straight into heat—equivalent to running nearly a thousand household space heaters inside an enclosed concrete room! Closed-loop air coolers carry that heat safely away into water pipes.

engineeringParameters.label: Heat rejection duty
engineeringParameters.valueText: Heat rejection duty (typically `~1.5–3.0%` of rated MW, i.e., `~0.7–1.4 MW` thermal heat removed on a `45 MW` unit!)

physicalLocation: Cylindrical outer steel/concrete enclosure on the powerhouse generator floor surrounding `comp-stator`, `comp-rotor`, and `comp-cooling-system`.
purpose: Form a sealed closed-loop ventilation chamber for cooling air, attenuate acoustic noise, protect personnel from high-voltage windings and high-speed rotating parts, and support upper bearing bridges and auxiliary sensors.
engineeringPrinciple: Sealed structural pressure/containment shell engineered for low acoustic transmission, dust/moisture exclusion (preventing airborne contaminants from fouling HV windings), and fire-containment safety (`CO2` or water-mist suppression integration).
constructionAndMaterials: Rolled structural steel cylindrical barrel (or concrete-lined pit barrel with removable steel upper deck covers/hatches), reinforced access doors with safety interlocks, acoustic insulation liner, and observation/fire-suppression ports.
operatingMechanism: Passive structural and airflow boundary keeping chilled recirculated air contained and guided strictly through stator cooling ducts and heat exchangers rather than leaking into the generator hall.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Keep access doors dogged tight during operation so cooling airflow pressure drops don't short-circuit ventilation; verify fire-interlock dampers before startup.
potentialFailureModes: Door gasket deterioration causing hot-air leaks into powerhouse
panel rattle vibration
condensation drip onto stator end-turns if internal space heaters fail while idle
maintenanceConsiderations: Door seal inspection, internal anti-condensation heater function check during shutdowns, paint/corrosion maintenance, safety interlock verification
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* In a real hydro powerhouse hall, you rarely see the giant spinning rotor directly—this protective steel barrel seals in cooled air, blocks dust, contains noise, and keeps engineers safe from `11,000-volt` copper bars and moving multi-ton steel inside.

engineeringParameters.label: Housing outer diameter
engineeringParameters.valueText: Housing outer diameter (plant-dependent, illustrative `~7–9 m` barrel)

engineeringParameters.label: acoustic attenuation
engineeringParameters.valueText: acoustic attenuation (`< 85 dBA` at 1 m on floor)

physicalLocation: Terminal chamber mounted on the outer wall of `comp-generator-housing` (phase side and neutral star-point side).
purpose: Provide the insulated electrical transition point collecting three-phase high-current power leads from `comp-stator-winding` into external busbars while housing metering/protection current transformers (CTs) and surge arresters.
engineeringPrinciple: Three-phase star (wye) connected AC termination ($P_e = \sqrt{3} V_L I_L \cos\phi$) where neutral ends connect through a high-resistance or distribution-transformer grounding cubicle to limit single-line-to-ground fault currents and avoid destructive stator core iron burning.
constructionAndMaterials: Non-magnetic aluminum or stainless-steel terminal enclosure (prevents inductive eddy-current heating around heavy phase currents), glazed porcelain or epoxy stand-off bushings, bolted silver-plated copper terminal flags with flexible laminated copper expansion shunts, ring-type protection/metering CTs, and neutral-grounding transformer/resistor panel.
operatingMechanism: Stationary electrical junction conducting full three-phase generator output current (`~2.4–2.6 kA` at `11 kV` class) safely out of the housing while isolating mechanical vibration via flexible braided shunts.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Inspect thermal imaging of bolted joints for loose-connection hotspots; verify neutral grounding resistor continuity and PT/CT secondary shorting blocks.
potentialFailureModes: Loose terminal lug overheating/arcing
moisture condensation flashover across porcelain bushings
CT secondary open-circuit overvoltage
surge-arrester failure
maintenanceConsiderations: Infrared thermography during load runs, contact-resistance micro-ohm (Ductor) tests across bolted flex-links, bushing insulator cleaning, torque verification
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* Before electricity can head out to a national power grid, the generator's stator coils must tie together cleanly—three live phase leads carry outgoing power while the neutral ends meet in a controlled grounding path that protects the core during faults.

engineeringParameters.label: Rated line-to-line voltage
engineeringParameters.valueText: Rated line-to-line voltage (illustrative `11.0 kV` RMS, `50 Hz`)

engineeringParameters.label: Basic Impulse Insulation Level
engineeringParameters.valueText: Basic Impulse Insulation Level (`BIL`, e.g., `75–95 kV`)

alternativeNames: Isolated Phase Bus (IPB) / Segregated Phase Bus Duct
physicalLocation: Overhead or gallery-mounted metal-enclosed bus duct running between `comp-generator-terminal`, `comp-circuit-breaker`, and the low-voltage bushings of `comp-step-up-transformer`.
purpose: Conduct heavy three-phase AC power at generator terminal voltage cleanly and safely between the generator and step-up transformer with minimal resistive loss, phase-to-phase fault risk, and electromagnetic interference.
engineeringPrinciple: Low-resistance high-ampacity conductor sizing ($P_{\text{loss}} = 3 I_{\text{phase}}^2 R_{\text{ac}}$); in Isolated Phase Bus (IPB) construction, each phase conductor sits centered inside an individual grounded aluminum sheath so induced shield currents nearly cancel external magnetic fields around adjacent steel powerhouse beams and eliminate phase-to-phase short circuits.
constructionAndMaterials: Hollow tubular or channel-section aluminum or copper conductors supported by porcelain/epoxy post insulators inside weatherproof grounded aluminum enclosures, fitted with flexible braided expansion joints, desiccant breathers / pressurized dry-air systems, and tap-off leads for station service & excitation transformers.
operatingMechanism: Passive heavy-duty electrical highway bridging powerhouse indoor switchgear to the outdoor transformer bay.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Maintain dry, dust-free interior enclosure air (anti-condensation heaters or low-pressure dry air purge) to avoid insulator surface tracking.
potentialFailureModes: Insulator tracking flashover from moisture/condensation
support insulator cracking from short-circuit electrodynamic forces
overheating at improperly torqued flex-links
enclosure gasket leaks
maintenanceConsiderations: Thermography along enclosure joints, contact-resistance testing across bolted flex connectors, insulator cleaning and Megger insulation checks, heater continuity testing
educationalExplanation: *Why heavy aluminum tubes instead of flexible cables?* At `11 kV` and `45 MW`, the generator pushes roughly `2,400 amperes` per phase—far too massive for ordinary insulated cables. Rigid metal-enclosed busbars keep phases physically isolated and dissipate heat safely.

engineeringParameters.label: busbar thermal rise limit
engineeringParameters.valueText: busbar thermal rise limit (`<= 65 K` ambient rise per IEEE C37.23)

physicalLocation: Inline along `comp-busbar` between `comp-generator-terminal` and `comp-step-up-transformer` (or paired on the high-voltage switchyard bay side).
purpose: Synchronize the generator smoothly onto the live electrical grid, carry continuous load current safely, and interrupt massive normal or short-circuit fault currents within milliseconds to protect the generator and transformer.
engineeringPrinciple: **Controlled Arc Interruption at AC Current Zero-Crossing:** Pulling apart live contacts under thousands of amperes creates a superheated plasma arc. Vacuum interrupters or compressed `SF6` / clean-air blast chambers stretch, cool, and de-ionize the arc channel so dielectric strength recovers faster than the Transient Recovery Voltage (TRV) right at natural AC zero-crossing ($i(t) = 0$ occurring `100 times/s` at `50 Hz`). Synchronizing relays close contacts ONLY when generator voltage magnitude, frequency, and phase angle match the grid (`Δθ ≈ 0°`).
constructionAndMaterials: Three-pole interrupter chambers (vacuum bottles or `SF6`/gas puffer poles), silver/copper-tungsten main and arcing contacts, spring-hydraulic stored-energy operating mechanism, current transformers, and parallel surge capacitors / disconnect switches.
operatingMechanism: Remains open during turbine startup and speed ramp until automatic synchronizer verifies phase match (`< ±5°`), then snaps closed in `~40–60 ms`. On protective relay trip (differential, overcurrent, reverse power, overspeed), trip coil releases stored spring energy to interrupt full fault current in `2–3` AC cycles (`~40–60 ms`).
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Out-of-phase closing causes catastrophic shaft torsional shock and transformer winding collapse; monitor gas pressure / vacuum integrity and trip-coil supervision continuously.
potentialFailureModes: Contact erosion after repeated fault trips
trip-coil open circuit or mechanism spring latch failure ("breaker failure")
`SF6` seal leak / vacuum loss
pole-discrepancy (one phase failing to close/open)
maintenanceConsiderations: Contact timing & travel-curve analyzer tests, static/dynamic contact resistance measurement, gas dew-point/purity checks (if gas-insulated) or vacuum bottle hi-pot checks, trip/close coil battery testing
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* You cannot just turn off `45 MW` of spinning electrical power with a household light switch—air would explode into an arc flash. A generator circuit breaker traps and extinguishes that arc safely inside `~0.05 seconds` at the exact instant AC current crosses zero.

engineeringParameters.label: generator-fed faults exhibit high DC-offset asymmetry requiring
engineeringParameters.valueText: generator-fed faults exhibit high DC-offset asymmetry requiring special IEEE C37.013 GCB duty)

physicalLocation: Concrete outdoor transformer bay immediately outside the powerhouse wall, between the generator busbar exit and `comp-switchyard`.
purpose: Transform generated medium-voltage, high-current AC (`~11 kV`) into high-voltage, low-current AC (`~110–220 kV` class) so bulk power transmits long distances with drastically reduced $I^2R$ line losses.
engineeringPrinciple: **Mutual Electromagnetic Induction & Joule Heating Reduction:** $$\frac{V_2}{V_1} = \frac{N_2}{N_1}, \qquad I_2 = I_1 \frac{N_1}{N_2} \text{ (ideal)}, \qquad P_{\text{line,loss}} = 3 I_2^2 R_{\text{line}} \propto \frac{1}{V_2^2}$$ Stepping voltage up `10×` (e.g., `11 kV → 110 kV`) or `20×` (`11 kV → 220 kV`) drops transmission current by `10×` or `20×`—cutting resistive line heat losses by **`100×` or `400×`**!
constructionAndMaterials: Three-limb grain-oriented electrical steel core, concentric copper primary (Delta) and secondary (Wye-grounded) windings, thermally upgraded Kraft paper insulation immersed in insulating mineral or ester transformer oil inside a heavy welded steel tank, external radiator fin banks with cooling fans (`ONAN/ONAF`), conservator expansion tank with Buchholz gas relay, HV porcelain/composite condenser bushings, and fire-containment oil pit.
operatingMechanism: Stationary electromagnetic device operating continuously near `~99.2–99.7%` efficiency; dissipates small no-load core magnetization losses and load-dependent copper $I^2R$ losses via oil thermosyphon circulation through radiator banks.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Monitor top-oil and winding hot-spot temperatures, dissolved gas analysis (DGA) for arcing/overheating indicators, tap-changer position (off-circuit or on-load), and Buchholz relay gas alarms.
potentialFailureModes: Winding insulation breakdown from moisture or lightning/switching surge
turn-to-turn short circuit triggering Buchholz/differential trip
HV bushing oil leak or partial discharge explosion
radiator fan/pump cooling fault
maintenanceConsiderations: Periodic oil Dissolved Gas Analysis (DGA), moisture/dielectric breakdown tests, Doble bushing & winding tan-delta testing, Sweep Frequency Response Analysis (SFRA), silica-gel breather drying, thermography
educationalExplanation: *Why step voltage up so high?* Because wire heat loss grows with the **square of current** ($I^2R$). Carrying `45 MW` over 50 km at `11 kV` (`~2,360 A`) would waste tens of percent heating the air; stepping up to `132 kV` drops current to `~197 A`, slashing line losses by over **`144×`**!
