engineeringParameters.label: voltage ratio
engineeringParameters.valueText: voltage ratio (illustrative `11 kV / 132 kV` or `11 kV / 220 kV`, plant-dependent)

physicalLocation: Fenced gravel-surfaced outdoor high-voltage yard adjacent to the transformer bay and take-off transmission gantry.
purpose: Safely switch, meter, protect, and route high-voltage power from the step-up transformer onto outgoing regional transmission lines while providing lightning surge arrest and visible maintenance isolation.
engineeringPrinciple: Air-insulated high-voltage phase clearances (governed by BIL and phase-to-ground/phase-to-phase dielectric breakdown margins), busbar buswork redundancy (e.g., single-bus, breaker-and-a-half, or ring-bus topologies), instrument transformer voltage/current scaling (`PT/CVT` & `CT`) for protective relaying, and metal-oxide varistor (MOV) surge clamping.
constructionAndMaterials: Crushed stone grounding grid surface (controls step-and-touch fault potentials), galvanized steel lattice portal gantries and equipment support stands, HV circuit breakers, motorized air-break disconnect switches, surge arresters, CTs, CVTs, aluminum tubular busbars, and protective ground mat.
operatingMechanism: Motorized disconnect switches provide visible air-gap isolation ONLY after HV breakers open; protective relays monitor differential, distance, and overvoltage faults across the yard.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Strict lock-out/tag-out interlocking prevents opening disconnect switches under load; vegetation/bird/insulator contamination flashover mitigation.
potentialFailureModes: Insulator pollution flashover in humid/coastal air
disconnect switch contact hot-spots
surge arrester thermal runaway
relay/DC battery auxiliary trip failure
maintenanceConsiderations: Infrared hotspot sweeps, breaker timing tests, insulator washing/RTV silicone coating, ground-grid impedance testing, protective relay secondary injection calibration
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* A switchyard is the traffic interchange between the power plant and the national grid—isolating faults in milliseconds, clamping lightning strikes, and safely decoupling equipment with visible open switches for maintenance crews.

engineeringParameters.label: Nominal system voltage
engineeringParameters.valueText: Nominal system voltage (`132 kV` / `220 kV` class, plant-dependent)

physicalLocation: Overhead steel lattice towers and catenary phase conductors departing `comp-switchyard` take-off gantry toward the regional grid corridor.
purpose: Transport high-voltage three-phase electrical energy efficiently across tens or hundreds of kilometers from the remote hydroelectric river gorge to population and industrial load centers.
engineeringPrinciple: Three-phase AC power transfer across transmission line reactance ($P \approx \frac{V_s V_r}{X} \sin\delta$), balancing resistive Joule losses ($I^2 R$), corona discharge limits, sag-tension mechanical catenary physics, and thermal ampacity.
constructionAndMaterials: Aluminum Conductor Steel Reinforced (`ACSR`) stranded phase conductors (aluminum outer strands for conductivity + steel inner core for tensile strength), overhead ground/shield wires (OPGW) above phases for lightning diversion, glass/ceramic/polymer suspension insulator strings, and galvanized steel lattice towers anchored on concrete foundations.
operatingMechanism: Passive electromagnetic wave/power corridor carrying active (`MW`) and reactive (`MVAR`) power continuously in phase equilibrium with grid impedance.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Conductor thermal sag increases during high ambient heat + heavy current; wind-induced aeolian vibration and galloping; lightning trip auto-reclose coordination.
potentialFailureModes: Lightning back-flashover across insulator strings
tree encroachment / phase-to-ground fault
extreme ice/wind mechanical tower loading
corroded splice overheating
maintenanceConsiderations: Helicopter/drone LiDAR clearance & corona UV/IR inspections, insulator string integrity testing, tower foundation & guy inspection, vegetation corridor clearing
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* Hydroelectric plants sit where valleys and rivers exist—often far from cities. High-voltage ACSR lines carry power over long distances with minimal loss using thin overhead shield wires above to intercept lightning before it strikes the live phases below.

engineeringParameters.label: phase conductor configuration and ground clearance.
engineeringParameters.valueText: phase conductor configuration and ground clearance.

physicalLocation: Downstream boundary node at the far end of `comp-transmission-line` representing the interconnected synchronous power system and consumer loads.
purpose: Represent the external synchronized alternating-current system that absorbs generated electricity, sets nominal grid frequency (`50 Hz` or `60 Hz`), and imposes dynamic consumer electrical load demand (`requestedLoadW`).
engineeringPrinciple: **Active Power Balance & Frequency Lock:** Across an interconnected AC grid, total instantaneous generation must continuously match total consumer load plus losses ($\sum P_{\text{gen}} = \sum P_{\text{load}} + P_{\text{loss}}$). Because a single plant (`~45 MW`) couples synchronously into a much larger grid, grid frequency (`50 Hz`) dictates the rotor's locked synchronous speed (`250 rpm`), while load demand governs electrical torque opposing the turbine.
constructionAndMaterials: Conceptual representation of substations, interconnected generation plants, distribution transformers, and industrial/residential end-use loads beyond the plant fence.
operatingMechanism: Requests active power (`requestedLoadW` in DENRYU Simulator). If available plant generation (`electricalGeneratedPowerW`) is less than requested load, a **power deficit** exists (`deliveredElectricalPowerW = available`); in a real grid, other plants must pick up the deficit or frequency sags / under-frequency load shedding occurs.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Generator governor droop response (`~4–5%` typical) helps share sudden system frequency deviations across interconnected hydro units smoothly.
potentialFailureModes: External grid short-circuit faults, voltage collapse, frequency excursions outside protection relay limits (`e.g., < 47.5 Hz` or `> 51.5 Hz`), loss-of-synchronism / islanding events
maintenanceConsiderations: Out of plant direct maintenance scope
coordinated through Regional Grid Dispatch / System Operator protection settings and telemetry tests
educationalExplanation: *Crucial misconception corrected:* Beginners often assume increasing electrical load slows down a hydro generator arbitrarily—or reducing water makes it spin at half speed while still on the grid. In reality, once synchronized to a large electrical grid, magnetic lock holds the generator strictly at `50 Hz` (`250 rpm`); changing load changes mechanical **torque** and guide-vane **flow demand**, not steady-state RPM!

engineeringParameters.label: requested plant dispatch load
engineeringParameters.valueText: requested plant dispatch load (`requestedLoadW`, default `40.0 MW` vs. `~44 MW` nominal output)

physicalLocation: Downstream submerged powerhouse wall exit where `comp-draft-tube` emerges horizontally into `comp-tailrace`.
purpose: Release low-velocity water smoothly below the minimum tailwater surface without allowing external air backflow into the draft tube, and house stoplog slots for turbine dewatering.
engineeringPrinciple: Submerged exit hydraulic seal: submerging the outlet soffit safely below minimum tailwater elevation ensures continuous liquid column vacuum integrity inside the draft tube diffuser while minimizing exit kinetic loss ($\frac{v_{\text{exit}}^2}{2g}$ kept small, typically `< 1–2%` of gross head).
constructionAndMaterials: Reinforced concrete twin or single rectangular exit portal bays divided by streamlined structural splitter piers, embedded stainless/painted steel stoplog guide slots, and overhead gantry crane / monorail hoist deck for stoplog gate placement.
operatingMechanism: Continuously submerged underwater outlet during generation; stoplog gates drop down into vertical slots solely during turbine inspection outages so dewatering pumps can empty the draft tube and spiral casing safely.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Never drop stoplogs under flowing conditions unless specifically designed as emergency closure gates; check differential water pressure before lifting stoplogs after maintenance.
potentialFailureModes: Stoplog guide siltation preventing tight seal during dewatering
concrete spalling around pier noses
uneven exit flow circulation if one bay clogs
maintenanceConsiderations: Stoplog rubber J-seal replacement, underwater concrete/guide slot cleaning before planned outages, overhead stoplog crane inspection
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* Notice that the draft tube outlet stays completely underwater—if air could sneak backward up into the draft tube, the vacuum suction underneath the turbine runner would break immediately and efficiency would plunge.

engineeringParameters.label: Outlet exit velocity
engineeringParameters.valueText: Outlet exit velocity (typically `~1.5–2.8 m/s`, substantially slower than runner exit)

engineeringParameters.label: minimum tailwater submergence above outlet crown
engineeringParameters.valueText: minimum tailwater submergence above outlet crown (`>= 0.5–1.5 m`).

physicalLocation: Engineered open channel extending immediately downstream from `comp-draft-tube-outlet` (and adjacent to spillway stilling apron) out toward the natural river.
purpose: Convey turbined discharge smoothly away from the powerhouse without backing up tailwater elevation (which would steal net head) while absorbing turbulence before rejoining the natural river channel.
engineeringPrinciple: Open-channel subcritical flow (Manning's equation $Q = \frac{1}{n} A R_h^{2/3} S^{1/2}$): wide, gently sloped cross-section keeps tailwater elevation stable and defines the downstream reference datum ($Z_{\text{tailwater}}$) determining gross plant head ($H_{\text{gross}} = Z_{\text{headwater}} - Z_{\text{tailwater}}$).
constructionAndMaterials: Excavated rock or reinforced concrete trapezoidal/rectangular channel with riprap bank stabilization, training walls separating powerhouse outflow from spillway turbulence, and tailwater level gauging staff/transducer.
operatingMechanism: Continuously collects steady outflow from the draft tube outlet and regulates downstream backpressure elevation naturally via channel geometry and river stage.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Rapid flow increases from `0 → 60 m³/s` during unit load pick-up create mild downstream surge waves; high river floods raise tailwater elevation, temporarily reducing available `Net Head (H)`.
potentialFailureModes: Sediment bar deposition or rockslide raising tailwater elevation (reducing head and power output)
bank erosion/undercutting during spillway co-discharge
maintenanceConsiderations: Periodic bathymetric dredging of gravel bars, riprap slope repair, tailwater level sensor calibration
educationalExplanation: *General principle:* Every meter that water backs up in the tailrace is one full meter of net head stolen directly from the turbine. Keeping the tailrace wide, deep, and unobstructed preserves maximum head across the Francis runner.

engineeringParameters.label: Tailwater elevation
engineeringParameters.valueText: Tailwater elevation ($Z_{\text{tw}}$, illustrative `~395 m` ASL, `90 m` below `485 m` headwater)

physicalLocation: Downstream riverbed beyond the plant tailrace and spillway stilling apron limits.
purpose: Return turbined (and any bypassed spillway) water cleanly back into the natural river ecosystem with preserved water volume, controlled velocity, and environmental flow continuity.
engineeringPrinciple: **Conservation of Mass (Non-Consumptive Energy Extraction):** Hydroelectric power extracts **gravitational potential and pressure energy**, NOT water molecules! Mass flow leaving the plant equals mass flow entering ($Q_{\text{out}} = Q_{\text{in}}$ in steady state), returning oxygen-managed water downstream for ecology, agriculture, and downstream communities.
constructionAndMaterials: Natural river morphology stabilized near the plant exit with river-training riprap and ecological monitoring gauging stations.
operatingMechanism: Passive downstream river boundary receiving steady tailrace flow and periodic spillway flood releases.
typicalOperatingConsiderations: Abrupt load rejections or rapid turbine startups cause downstream river level fluctuations; plants obey strict environmental ramping schedules.
potentialFailureModes: Downstream riverbank erosion, rapid-ramping aquatic stranding (operational/environmental risk), gravel bar migration altering tailwater rating curve
maintenanceConsiderations: Downstream stream-gauge calibration, environmental dissolved-oxygen/temperature monitoring, bank stabilization checks
educationalExplanation: *Closing engineering lesson:* Unlike coal or gas plants that burn fuel into exhaust gases, a hydroelectric plant does not consume water—it simply borrows water's elevation drop, converts that gravitational potential into electricity inside the Francis unit, and gives every drop back to the river downstream.

engineeringParameters.label: river ramping rate limits
engineeringParameters.valueText: river ramping rate limits (how rapidly discharge can increase/decrease to protect downstream river safety & aquatic habitat).
